title: CML, Sharpe ratio, CAPM and the SML

topics.title: Adding the risk-free asset
topics.summary: Once a risk-free asset exists, an investor can mix any risky portfolio with it. The mix lies on a straight capital allocation line whose slope is the Sharpe ratio, and the steepest such line, tangent to the efficient frontier, is the capital market line through the market portfolio M.

topics.title: Systematic risk and beta
topics.summary: Total risk splits into a diversifiable (unsystematic) part and a non-diversifiable (systematic) part. Beta measures the systematic part as a regression slope against the market, and the beta of a portfolio is simply the weighted average of its betas, with a zero for the risk-free asset.

topics.title: CAPM and the SML
topics.summary: Only systematic risk is rewarded: the CAPM says expected return = risk-free rate + beta × market risk premium. The security market line draws this, alpha shows which assets are under- or overpriced, and the course ends by separating σ from β, building portfolios stage by stage, and linking the required return to a project's cost of capital.

concepts.term: Risk-free asset and the capital allocation line (CAL)
concepts.definition: The risk-free asset pays a certain return R_F with σ_F = 0. Mixing it with a risky portfolio P (weights w_F + w_P = 1) gives E[R] = w_P E[R_P] + w_F R_F and σ = w_P σ_P, so every mix lies on a straight line from R_F through P: the capital allocation line (CAL).
concepts.explain: Because σ_F = 0, the variance and correlation terms for the risk-free asset drop out of the two-asset σ formula and only w_P σ_P is left: risk rises in direct proportion to the weight in P, and return is linear in the weights, hence a straight line. Lending (w_F > 0) puts you between R_F and P; borrowing at R_F (w_F < 0, so w_P > 1) puts you beyond P. The professor assumes the lending and borrowing rates are equal.
concepts.contrast: CAL: one risky portfolio P plus R_F, a straight line. Efficient frontier: a curve of risky assets only. CML: the special CAL tangent to the frontier (through M). SML: a different picture (E[R] against β, not σ). Two risky assets give a curved σ_P; one risky portfolio plus R_F gives a straight line.
concepts.trap: Forgetting the risk-free weight in E[R] (using w_P E[R_P] alone); entering borrowing as a positive weight so the weights no longer sum to 1; trying to use the full two-asset σ formula with ρ. Dollars are not weights: divide by your own wealth, so $60,000 in P on $40,000 of wealth is w_P = 1.5.
concepts.mnemonic: σ_F = 0 wipes out the correlation: σ is just w_P × σ_P.
concepts.formula: E[R] = w_P E[R_P] + (1 − w_P) R_F;  σ = w_P σ_P  (w_F = 1 − w_P; w_F < 0 means borrowing)

concepts.term: Sharpe ratio and the capital market line (CML)
concepts.definition: Sharpe ratio = tan φ = (E[R_P] − R_F)/σ_P: the excess return (risk premium) per unit of total risk, equal to the slope of P's CAL. The best CAL is tangent to the efficient frontier at the market portfolio M and is the capital market line (CML): E[R_A] = R_F + [(E[R_M] − R_F)/σ_M] σ_A for any efficient portfolio A.
concepts.explain: A steeper CAL dominates a flatter one: on the steeper line you can find a point with more return at the same σ. So the portfolio with the higher Sharpe ratio is better, even if its raw return is lower. Mixing a portfolio with R_F never changes its Sharpe ratio, you only slide along the same CAL. The CML turns the market's Sharpe ratio into a price list: the required E[R] of any efficient portfolio given its σ.
concepts.example: R_F = 3%. Fund P: E[R] = 10%, σ = 14% gives Sharpe 7/14 = 0.50. Fund Q: E[R] = 12%, σ = 20% gives 9/20 = 0.45. P has the steeper CAL, so P wins despite Q's higher return. If M has E[R_M] = 9% and σ_M = 12% (slope 0.50), an efficient portfolio with σ = 18% should earn 3 + 0.50 × 18 = 12%.
concepts.contrast: Sharpe divides by σ (total risk) and ranks whole portfolios; the SML's reward-to-risk divides by β (systematic risk) and prices individual assets. CML: E[R] against σ, efficient portfolios only. SML: E[R] against β, every asset and portfolio.
concepts.trap: Putting β (or σ_M) in the denominator; forgetting to subtract R_F in the numerator; using the CML to price a single stock (it carries diversifiable risk, so it plots below the CML); choosing the fund with the higher return instead of the higher Sharpe ratio.
concepts.mnemonic: Sharpe = slope = excess return per unit of σ.
concepts.formula: Sharpe = tan φ = (E[R_P] − R_F)/σ_P;  CML: E[R_A] = R_F + [(E[R_M] − R_F)/σ_M] σ_A

concepts.term: Market portfolio and the index proxy
concepts.definition: The market portfolio M is the risky portfolio at the point where the CAL from R_F is tangent to the efficient frontier: it has the highest Sharpe ratio of any risky portfolio, and the tangent line is the CML. In practice we proxy M with a broad index portfolio (S&P 500 / SPDR trust; the S&P/TSX Composite in Canada). By definition β_M = 1.
concepts.explain: To find M, start at R_F and rotate a straight line upward until it just touches the frontier: the single point of contact is M. In theory every investor holds M plus R_F and chooses only the weight w_F, according to risk tolerance. M is hard to find in advance (it depends on future expected returns and σ's, and the best past portfolio need not be the best future one), so we use a broad index as a stand-in.
concepts.example: R_F = 2%. Three frontier portfolios: P1 has E[R] = 8%, σ = 10% (Sharpe 0.60); P2 has 10%, 14% (0.571); P3 has 13%, 20% (0.55). P1 has the steepest CAL of the three, so it is the best of these candidates to mix with R_F (M's own Sharpe ratio is at least 0.60). A timid and a bold investor would both hold M; the timid one adds T-bills, the bold one borrows.
concepts.contrast: M is the maximum-Sharpe (tangency) portfolio. It is not the minimum-variance portfolio (lowest σ, far left of the frontier) and not the highest-expected-return portfolio (far right). An index fund is a proxy for M, not M itself.
concepts.trap: 'Tangent' is not 'highest return' or 'lowest σ'. The review question 'How do we find the market portfolio?' wants: draw the CAL from R_F tangent to the efficient frontier. When asked which candidate portfolio is best to combine with R_F, compute each Sharpe ratio and pick the highest. Remember the index is only a proxy.
concepts.mnemonic: Touch once, tangent: that touch is M.
concepts.formula: Sharpe_M = (E[R_M] − R_F)/σ_M is the maximum of all risky portfolios;  β_M = 1

concepts.definition: Total risk (measured by σ) = systematic risk + unsystematic risk. Systematic (market, non-diversifiable) risk affects all assets; unsystematic (company-specific, diversifiable, idiosyncratic) risk affects one asset or a small group. Diversification removes only the unsystematic part, so a well-diversified portfolio's σ falls to a limit of σ_M.
concepts.explain: Systematic: surprises that hit almost every firm, such as GDP, inflation and interest rates. Unsystematic: a strike, lawsuit, fire, new product or CEO change at one company. In a big portfolio the good and bad company-specific surprises cancel, but a market-wide surprise moves everything the same way, so it stays. Only unexpected news is risk: news already expected is already in prices. Because unsystematic risk can be removed almost free, the market pays no premium for it (the systematic risk principle).
concepts.example: In the textbook's classic study of randomly chosen NYSE stocks (Table 13.7), one stock has an average σ of about 49%; with 10 stocks σ falls to about 24%, with 100 to about 20% and with 1,000 to about 19%. That floor is systematic risk, roughly the σ of the market (the lecture's picture of σ_P falling to σ_M). A fire at one packaging plant is unsystematic; an unexpected Bank of Canada rate hike is systematic.
concepts.contrast: Systematic = market = non-diversifiable. Unsystematic = company-specific = diversifiable = non-systematic = unique = idiosyncratic. Do not confuse either with total risk σ (the sum of both parts) or with β (the measure of the systematic part only).
concepts.trap: Cue words: 'affects the whole economy / all firms' means systematic; 'a single company / small group' means unsystematic. Do not say diversification removes all risk, and do not say the market rewards total risk. Only the surprise part of news is risk, so a fully expected rate change does not move prices.
concepts.mnemonic: System-wide = Systematic. Diversify away the Unique.
concepts.formula: Total risk = systematic risk + unsystematic risk;  σ_P → σ_M as the number of stocks grows

concepts.term: Beta: a measure of systematic risk
concepts.definition: β_i = cov(R_i, R_M)/σ_M² = ρ_iM σ_i/σ_M: the slope of the regression of the asset's returns on the market's returns, measuring systematic risk. β_M = 1 and β_F = 0. Unlike the correlation ρ, β is not limited to the range −1 to +1.
concepts.explain: Beta says how much the stock moves, on average, for a 1% market move. In the regression R_i = α + β R_M + ε the slope is β. Divide by the market's variance σ_M², not by σ_M. Because β = ρ × (σ_i/σ_M), a stock can be highly correlated with the market and still have a small β if it swings much less than the market, or a β above 1 if it swings more. Providers publish different betas because they choose different market indexes, time windows, return frequencies and adjustments.
concepts.contrast: β vs ρ: ρ (−1 to +1) measures how tightly two assets move together; β also scales for relative size, σ_i/σ_M. β vs σ: β is systematic risk only, σ is total risk. β vs α: slope versus intercept of the same regression.
concepts.trap: Dividing the covariance by σ_M instead of σ_M² (the most common slip); putting σ_i in the denominator (inverting the σ ratio); reporting ρ as β; mixing percent and decimals when squaring σ_M (18% means 0.18² = 0.0324). A beta of 0 does not mean σ = 0.
concepts.mnemonic: β = ρ × (stock σ ÷ market σ); divide by the market's VARIANCE.

concepts.definition: β_P = Σ w_i β_i: the weighted average of the asset betas, with β_F = 0 for the risk-free asset and β_M = 1. The weights, including the risk-free weight, must sum to 1; a negative risk-free weight means borrowing at R_F, which pushes β_P above the beta of the risky holdings.
concepts.explain: Unlike portfolio σ, portfolio beta needs no correlations: it is a weighted average, like portfolio return. To build a target beta, put the known holdings in, solve for the unknown stock's weight, and let the risk-free asset (β = 0) absorb the rest: w_F = 1 − all other weights. If the target beta is higher than the betas you can hold, you must borrow (w_F < 0).
concepts.example: A $60,000 portfolio: $20,000 in a utility (β = 0.60), $30,000 in a bank (β = 1.10) and $10,000 in T-bills. Weights 1/3, 1/2 and 1/6, so β_P = 0.3333 × 0.60 + 0.5 × 1.10 + 0.1667 × 0 = 0.20 + 0.55 = 0.75. To lift the beta to 1.5 with the bank stock alone you would need w = 1.5/1.10 = 1.364 and w_F = −0.364 (borrowing).
concepts.contrast: β_P is linear in the weights; σ_P is not (it needs ρ). A risk-free holding has β = 0 but still has a weight. A long-only stock portfolio with no risk-free asset cannot have a beta below its lowest stock beta or above its highest.
concepts.trap: Dropping the T-bill (or the borrowing) from the weights so they no longer sum to 1; using dollars instead of weights; entering borrowing as a positive weight; giving the T-bill a beta of 1; taking the simple average of the betas.
concepts.mnemonic: Weights × betas; the risk-free asset is a zero, not a nobody.
concepts.formula: β_P = Σ w_i β_i  (β_F = 0, β_M = 1, Σ w_i = 1 including w_F)

concepts.definition: CAPM: E[R_i] = R_F + β_i (E[R_M] − R_F), equivalently E[R_i] − R_F = β_i (E[R_M] − R_F): the stock's risk premium is its β times the market risk premium. Expected return = time value of money + (amount of systematic risk × price of systematic risk).
concepts.explain: Three parts: R_F pays for waiting; E[R_M] − R_F is the market risk premium (the price of one unit of β); β is how many units you carry. Only systematic risk is priced, so σ never appears. Because E[R] is also the required return, it is the discount rate for an asset of that risk. You can rearrange for β, R_F or E[R_M].
concepts.example: R_F = 4.5%, E[R_M] = 10%, β = 0.8 (the style of the sample exam). Market risk premium = 10 − 4.5 = 5.5%, so E[R] = 4.5 + 0.8 × 5.5 = 8.9%.
concepts.contrast: Market return E[R_M] vs market risk premium E[R_M] − R_F (if the question gives the premium, do not subtract R_F again). CAPM vs SML: the same equation; the SML is its graph with β on the horizontal axis. CAPM vs CML: the CML uses σ and efficient portfolios only.
concepts.trap: Writing R_F + β × E[R_M] (no subtraction of R_F); treating the market risk premium as the market return or the reverse; percent and decimal mix-ups; solving for R_F, which appears twice in the equation.

concepts.term: Security market line, alpha and mispricing
concepts.definition: The security market line (SML) plots E[R] against β: intercept R_F, slope E[R_M] − R_F, passing through the market at β = 1. Alpha α = the E[R] an asset offers − the E[R] CAPM requires for its β. Above the SML (α > 0) means undervalued; below (α < 0) means overvalued. In equilibrium every asset has the same reward-to-risk ratio (E[R_i] − R_F)/β_i.
concepts.explain: An asset above the SML pays more than its β justifies: investors buy, its price rises, and its expected return falls back onto the line. Below the line the reverse happens. Equal reward-to-risk lets you solve for R_F or the market risk premium from two assets: set (E[R_a] − R_F)/β_a = (E[R_b] − R_F)/β_b and cross-multiply. A positive-NPV investment plots above the SML.
concepts.example: R_F = 3% and market risk premium 6%. A stock with β = 1.2 offering 11%: CAPM says 3 + 1.2 × 6 = 10.2%, so α = 11 − 10.2 = +0.8%, above the SML, undervalued. Reward-to-risk: (11 − 3)/1.2 = 6.67% > 6%.
concepts.contrast: Above the SML = undervalued (cheap, price will rise), not overvalued. Alpha is a gap in return; beta is risk. SML (β axis, all assets) vs CML (σ axis, efficient portfolios).
concepts.trap: Alpha sign reversed; saying a stock above the SML will fall in price; comparing reward-to-risk using σ instead of β; algebra slips when solving for R_F (cross-multiply, collect the R_F terms).
concepts.mnemonic: Above the line = a bargain: price up, return falls back to the line.
concepts.formula: α = E[R_i] − [R_F + β_i (E[R_M] − R_F)];  (E[R_i] − R_F)/β_i = E[R_M] − R_F = SML slope

concepts.term: σ ≠ β: which risk measure to use when
concepts.definition: σ measures total risk (systematic + unsystematic); β measures only systematic risk. The risk that earns a premium, and that matters to a well-diversified investor, is β; σ matters to someone holding a single stock and to the ranking of whole portfolios by Sharpe ratio.
concepts.explain: The professor uses two measures of risk: σ for volatility and β for systematic risk. A stock can be very volatile yet have a low β (much of its risk is unsystematic and can be diversified away), so its expected return is low. Which stock is 'riskier' depends on who is asking: an investor with all her money in one stock cares about σ; a diversified investor cares about β.
concepts.example: Stock A: σ = 40%, β = 0.5. Stock B: σ = 20%, β = 1.5. A has the greater total risk, so also more unsystematic risk; B has three times the systematic risk, so B has the higher risk premium and expected return under CAPM.
concepts.contrast: σ vs β: total vs systematic. Sharpe (σ in the denominator, ranks portfolios) vs reward-to-risk (β in the denominator, prices assets). E[R]-σ diagram (CML) vs SML.
concepts.trap: Ranking expected returns by σ; calling the high-σ stock 'riskier' for a diversified investor; plugging σ into the CAPM. 'Which has the higher expected return?' means look at β. 'Which has more total risk?' means look at σ.
concepts.mnemonic: Alone, look at σ. In a crowd, look at β.

concepts.term: Building a portfolio: σ, then ρ, then β
concepts.definition: The professor's recipe: for your first stock choose low σ; for your next few stocks choose low ρ with what you already hold (diversification benefit); when adding to an already well-diversified portfolio choose low β and positive α.
concepts.explain: Each stage uses the risk measure that matters at that stage. With one stock all its risk is yours, so look at σ. With a few stocks the biggest gain comes from risk that cancels, so look at ρ with your existing holdings. Once the portfolio is diversified, only systematic risk is left, so only β changes your risk; a positive α adds return without extra systematic risk.
concepts.example: Maya owns no stocks, so she starts with a low-σ utility. Next she adds a Saskatchewan potash miner and a Vancouver software firm because their ρ with the utility is low. With 30 holdings she adds a new stock only if its β is low (to hold down systematic risk) and its α is positive.
concepts.contrast: σ is for the first stock, ρ for the next few, β (with α) for a diversified portfolio. Do not choose the first stock by low β (a low-β stock can still be very volatile), and do not use ρ with the market when ρ among your own holdings is what matters.
concepts.trap: Using σ when the portfolio is already diversified; using ρ at stage 3; ignoring α (a low β with a negative α hurts return); saying β matters for a one-stock investor.
concepts.mnemonic: σ, ρ, β: the stage decides the measure.

concepts.term: Link to the cost of capital
concepts.definition: From the investor's side E[R] is the required return; from the firm's side the same number is the cost of capital for an investment of that risk. CAPM gives it: k = R_F + β_project (E[R_M] − R_F). A project is worth doing when its expected return (the IRR, for conventional cash flows) exceeds k, i.e. when it plots above the SML (positive NPV).
concepts.explain: All investments of similar risk should offer similar returns. A firm should discount a project at the return investors can earn elsewhere at the same β, not at the interest rate on the loan used to pay for it. On this exam the idea shows up as: compute the CAPM rate, then decide.
concepts.example: R_F = 3.5% and market risk premium 6.2%. A project with β = 1.3 should be discounted at 3.5 + 1.3 × 6.2 = 11.56%. If its IRR is 13%, IRR > k: it plots above the SML, so accept (NPV > 0).
concepts.contrast: Required return k (from CAPM, depends on the project's risk) vs expected return IRR (what the project promises). Project β vs the firm's overall β: use the project's own. Cost of capital vs the cost of the particular financing source.
concepts.trap: Using the firm's average rate for a riskier project; comparing the IRR with R_F instead of the CAPM rate; thinking a positive-NPV project plots below the SML.
concepts.mnemonic: Required return = what the SML pays for that β.
concepts.formula: k = R_F + β_project (E[R_M] − R_F);  accept if IRR > k

formulas.name: Mix of a risky portfolio and the risk-free asset (CAL)
formulas.formula: E[R] = w_P E[R_P] + (1 − w_P) R_F;  σ = w_P σ_P
formulas.when: Any combination of one risky portfolio P with the risk-free asset; w_P > 1 means borrowing at R_F.
formulas.trap: Forgetting the (1 − w_P) R_F term, or letting the weights sum to more than 1 when borrowing.

formulas.name: Sharpe ratio
formulas.when: Compare portfolios or CALs; the best CAL (highest Sharpe ratio) is tangent to the frontier at M.
formulas.trap: Uses σ, not β, in the denominator, and the excess return over R_F in the numerator.

formulas.name: Capital market line
formulas.when: Required return of an efficient portfolio with total risk σ_A, or the σ needed for a target return.
formulas.trap: Applies to efficient portfolios only, never to a single stock.

formulas.name: Beta from covariance
formulas.when: Beta from a state table (cov = Σ p (R_i − E[R_i])(R_M − E[R_M])) or from a stated covariance.
formulas.trap: The denominator is the market VARIANCE, not σ_M.

formulas.name: Beta from correlation
formulas.when: Beta from the correlation and the two standard deviations.
formulas.trap: σ_i on top, σ_M below; β is not bounded by ±1 like ρ.

formulas.name: Market-model regression
formulas.when: Interpret beta as the slope when stock returns are regressed on market returns.
formulas.trap: Beta is the slope, alpha the intercept; both come from the same line.

formulas.name: Portfolio beta
formulas.formula: β_P = Σ w_i β_i  (β_F = 0, β_M = 1, Σ w_i = 1)
formulas.when: Beta of any portfolio, including a risk-free weight; solve for an unknown weight to hit a target beta.
formulas.trap: Weights must include the risk-free (possibly negative) weight and add up to 1.

formulas.name: CAPM / SML
formulas.when: Expected or required return of any asset from its beta; also the equation of the SML.
formulas.trap: Subtract R_F from the market return first (or use the stated market risk premium directly).

formulas.name: CAPM rearranged for beta and the market return
formulas.formula: β_i = (E[R_i] − R_F)/(E[R_M] − R_F);  E[R_M] = R_F + (E[R_i] − R_F)/β_i
formulas.when: Back out the beta or the market return when the other inputs are given.
formulas.trap: A stated market risk premium is not E[R_M]; add R_F back to get the market return.

formulas.name: Reward-to-risk ratio and SML slope
formulas.when: Test whether an asset is on the SML; set two assets equal to solve for R_F or the market risk premium.
formulas.trap: A higher ratio than the market's means above the SML (undervalued).

formulas.name: Alpha
formulas.when: Mispricing: α > 0 plots above the SML (undervalued, price rises); α < 0 plots below it (overvalued).
formulas.trap: Offered return minus required return, in that order.

formulas.name: Total risk decomposition
formulas.formula: Total risk = systematic risk + unsystematic risk;  σ_P → σ_M as N grows
formulas.when: Explain what diversification removes and what remains.
formulas.trap: Diversification removes only the unsystematic part.

formulas.name: Project required return from CAPM
formulas.formula: k = R_F + β_project (E[R_M] − R_F);  accept if IRR > k
formulas.when: Discount rate for a project of a given systematic risk, then compare with the project's IRR.
formulas.trap: Use the project's own beta, not the firm's overall beta.

questions.stem: In the capital allocation line framework, which description fits the risk-free asset?
options: A certain return R_F with σ = 0, so it adds no variance or covariance term
A certain return R_F, but with a beta of 1 because it is part of the market
An asset whose expected return is zero and whose σ is also zero
An asset paying R_F with a small σ that diversification can remove
questions.explanation: The risk-free asset pays R_F for certain, so σ_F = 0. That is why the w_F², σ_F and correlation terms vanish from the portfolio σ formula. Its beta is 0, not 1, and R_F itself is positive, not zero.

questions.stem: Cypress Credit Union keeps one diversified equity fund P (not claimed to be the tangent portfolio) and only changes how much of its money sits in 90-day Government of Canada T-bills. The straight line of all the E[R] and σ combinations it can reach is called the:
options: capital market line (CML)
capital allocation line (CAL)
security market line (SML)
efficient frontier of risky assets
questions.explanation: Mixing one risky portfolio with the risk-free asset traces a straight capital allocation line. It would be the CML only if P were the tangent portfolio M. The SML plots E[R] against β, and the frontier is a curve of risky assets only.

questions.stem: Tamarack Capital puts 70% of its money in a risky portfolio P (E[R_P] = 9.5%, σ_P = 16.0%) and 30% in T-bills yielding 2.5%. What is the expected return of the combined portfolio?
questions.explanation: E[R] = w_P E[R_P] + w_F R_F = 0.70 × 9.5 + 0.30 × 2.5 = 6.65 + 0.75 = 7.40%. Dropping the risk-free term gives 6.65%; using 0.70 for both weights (they then add to 1.4) gives 8.40%; a simple average ignores the 70/30 split and gives 6.00%.

questions.stem: Prairie Endowment has $2,000,000. It places $1,400,000 in a diversified equity portfolio P (E[R_P] = 10.5%, σ_P = 18.0%) and the rest in T-bills paying 3.2%. Find both weights and the σ of the combined portfolio, then give its expected return (% per annum).

steps.label: σ of the mix = w_P σ_P

solution: σ = w_P σ_P = 0.70 × 18.0% = 12.6% (σ_F = 0, so no correlation term)

errors.label: Left out the T-bill term
errors.explain: The risk-free asset still earns R_F on its 30% weight: add w_F R_F.

errors.label: Averaged the two returns
errors.explain: The weights come from the dollars (70/30), not 50/50.

errors.label: Used dollars in millions as weights
errors.explain: 1.4 and 0.6 add to 2.0. Divide each amount by total wealth to get weights that sum to 1.

questions.explanation: Weights come from dollars over total wealth; σ = w_P σ_P because σ_F = 0; E[R] is the weighted average of E[R_P] and R_F.

questions.stem: Hanna has $40,000 of her own money. She borrows another $20,000 at the T-bill rate of 3.0% (borrowing and lending rates are equal) and invests all $60,000 in portfolio P with E[R_P] = 10.0% and σ_P = 15.0%. What is the σ of her position (% per annum)?

steps.label: Expected return on her own money
σ of her position = w_P σ_P

solution: σ = w_P σ_P = 1.50 × 15.0% = 22.5% (beyond P on the same CAL)

errors.label: Used σ_P without scaling for leverage
errors.explain: Investing 150% of her wealth in P scales σ by 1.5: σ = w_P σ_P.

errors.label: Used the risk-free weight as the weight on P
errors.explain: The weight on P is 1.50 (60,000/40,000), not 0.50.

questions.explanation: Leverage multiplies P's risk: with w_P = 1.5 the position sits 50% further out on the CAL, so σ = 1.5 × 15% = 22.5%.

questions.stem: Rocky View Pension can mix a risky portfolio P (E[R_P] = 11.5%, σ_P = 20.0%) with T-bills at 2.5%. The board wants the overall σ to be 14.0%. What expected return (% per annum) does the mix earn?
solution: Because σ = w_P σ_P, w_P = 14.0/20.0 = 0.70 and w_F = 0.30

errors.label: Inverted the weight: w_P = σ_P/σ_target
errors.explain: A target σ below σ_P means w_P < 1; the weight is σ_target/σ_P, not the reverse.

errors.label: Left out the T-bill term
errors.explain: Add w_F R_F = 0.30 × 2.5% for the T-bill portion.

questions.explanation: On a CAL σ is proportional to w_P, so w_P = σ_target/σ_P. The return follows from the weighted average.

questions.stem: Why is a capital allocation line (P mixed with the risk-free asset) a straight line?
options: Because R_F and P are perfectly positively correlated, so the usual two-asset curve collapses to a line
Because investors can lend at R_F but cannot borrow at it, so the line simply stops at portfolio P
Because the efficient frontier of risky assets is itself nearly straight near the point of tangency with the line
Because σ_F = 0, the σ formula collapses to σ = w_P σ_P, so σ and E[R] both move in proportion to w_P
questions.explanation: The two-asset σ formula has w_F²σ_F², and a correlation term times σ_F. With σ_F = 0 only w_P²σ_P² is left, so σ = w_P σ_P. Correlation is irrelevant because it multiplies zero; it is not that R_F is 'perfectly correlated' with P.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly contrasts a capital allocation line with the efficient frontier of risky stocks?
options: The CAL is a straight line using R_F; the frontier is a curve of risky assets only
Both are straight lines, but the CAL is steeper because it includes R_F
The frontier contains the risk-free asset, while the CAL contains only stocks
The CAL is curved because of correlation, while the frontier is straight because of diversification
questions.explanation: R_F has σ = 0, so mixing it with P gives a straight line. Mixing risky stocks gives a curve whose bend depends on correlation. The risk-free asset belongs to the CAL, not to the frontier of stocks.

questions.stem: A CAL built from a risky portfolio P and the risk-free asset has all of the following properties EXCEPT:
options: it passes through the point σ = 0, E[R] = R_F
its slope is the beta of P
points beyond P require borrowing at R_F (w_F < 0)
σ at any point equals w_P σ_P
questions.explanation: The slope of the CAL is the Sharpe ratio (E[R_P] − R_F)/σ_P = tan φ, not a beta. The other three statements are true: the intercept is R_F, w_F < 0 means borrowing, and σ = w_P σ_P.

questions.stem: Zainab likes portfolio P but wants a higher expected return than P offers, using only P and the risk-free asset (lending and borrowing rates equal). What should she do?
options: Lend more at R_F so that w_F rises above its current value
Switch to a single stock with a higher β but the same σ as P
Borrow at R_F and put more than 100% of her money in P (w_F < 0)
Hold P alone, since no mix of P and R_F can beat P itself
questions.explanation: Points beyond P on its CAL have w_P > 1, which means borrowing at R_F. E[R] rises because the borrowed money earns E[R_P] − R_F > 0 on top of her own, though σ rises too. Lending moves her toward R_F, lowering return.

questions.stem: An investor holds w_F = −0.40 in the risk-free asset and w_P = 1.40 in portfolio P. Which interpretation is correct?
options: She borrowed 40% of her wealth at R_F and holds 140% in P, so σ = 1.40 σ_P
She short-sold P and lent the proceeds at R_F, so her σ is 0.40 σ_P
She lent 40% of her wealth at R_F and holds 60% in P, so her σ is 0.60 σ_P
She holds 140% in P, which is possible only if R_F is higher than E[R_P]
questions.explanation: A negative risk-free weight is borrowing. The weights still sum to 1 (1.40 − 0.40), and σ = w_P σ_P = 1.40 σ_P. Lending would be a positive w_F.

questions.stem: Because the risk-free asset has σ_F = 0, the standard deviation of any mix of P and R_F simplifies to σ = _____.
options: w_P² σ_P²
w_P σ_P
w_P σ_P + w_F R_F
(w_P + w_F) σ_P
questions.explanation: In σ = √(w_F²σ_F² + w_P²σ_P² + 2ρ w_F σ_F w_P σ_P) the F terms are zero, leaving √(w_P²σ_P²) = w_P σ_P. The squared version is a variance; (w_P + w_F) σ_P would equal σ_P because the weights sum to 1.

questions.stem: Sofia has $50,000. She borrows $30,000 at the risk-free rate of 3.0% and invests the full $80,000 in portfolio P (E[R_P] = 10.4%, σ_P = 17.0%). What is the expected return on her own $50,000?
questions.explanation: w_P = 80/50 = 1.6 and w_F = −0.6, so E[R] = 1.6 × 10.4% − 0.6 × 3.0% = 16.64% − 1.80% = 14.84%. Ignoring the interest on the loan gives 16.64%; entering the borrowing as +0.6 (weights then add to 2.2) gives 18.44%; treating her as if she held P alone gives 10.40%.

questions.stem: If lending and borrowing rates are equal, the CAL continues as the same straight line beyond portfolio P.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Beyond P the weight on the risk-free asset is negative (borrowing at R_F), and σ = w_P σ_P and E[R] stay linear in w_P. In reality the borrowing rate is higher, which would bend the line, but the professor assumes equal rates.

questions.stem: The Sharpe ratio of a portfolio P is:
options: E[R_P]/σ_P, the raw return per unit of total risk
(E[R_P] − R_F)/β_P, the excess return per unit of systematic risk
(E[R_P] − R_F)/σ_P, the excess return per unit of total risk
(E[R_P] − R_F)/σ_P², the excess return per unit of variance
questions.explanation: Sharpe = tan φ = (E[R_P] − R_F)/σ_P: a risk premium divided by σ. Leaving out R_F gives a ratio that is not the CAL slope; dividing by β is the SML's reward-to-risk; dividing by variance mixes units.

questions.stem: On a diagram with σ on the horizontal axis and E[R] on the vertical axis, the slope of the straight line from R_F to portfolio P (tan φ) is called the:
options: Sharpe ratio of P
beta of P
market risk premium
correlation between P and the market
questions.explanation: The rise (E[R_P] − R_F) over the run σ_P is the Sharpe ratio. A beta would be the slope on a diagram with β on the horizontal axis (the SML).

questions.stem: Evergreen Growth Fund has an expected return of 10.4% per annum and σ = 15.2%; its beta is 1.25. Three-month T-bills yield 3.1%. What is the fund's Sharpe ratio?

errors.label: Did not subtract R_F
errors.explain: The numerator is the excess return over the risk-free rate.

errors.label: Divided by beta instead of σ
errors.explain: Sharpe uses total risk σ. Dividing by β gives the SML's reward-to-risk ratio, a different measure.

errors.label: Divided by the variance
errors.explain: The Sharpe ratio divides the excess return by σ, not by the variance σ².

questions.explanation: Sharpe ratio = excess return per unit of σ: (10.4 − 3.1)/15.2 = 0.48. The beta of 1.25 is not needed; dividing by it gives the SML's reward-to-risk ratio (5.84), not a Sharpe ratio.

questions.stem: T-bills yield 2.5%. Fund X has E[R] = 12.5% and σ = 21.0%. Fund Y has E[R] = 9.6% and σ = 12.0%. Either fund can be mixed with T-bills. What is the Sharpe ratio of the fund whose CAL is better?

steps.label: Sharpe ratio of Y (the steeper CAL)

solution: Y has the higher Sharpe ratio, so its CAL is steeper: 0.59

errors.label: Reported the Sharpe ratio of the higher-return fund
errors.explain: The better CAL belongs to the fund with the higher Sharpe ratio, not the higher raw return.

errors.label: Did not subtract R_F for Y

questions.explanation: A steeper CAL dominates a flatter one, so rank by Sharpe ratio. Y earns less than X but more excess return per unit of σ.

questions.stem: T-bills yield 2.6%. The market portfolio has E[R_M] = 9.8% and σ_M = 16.0%. According to the capital market line, what expected return (% per annum) should an efficient portfolio with σ = 21.0% offer?

steps.label: Slope of the CML = Sharpe ratio of M
Risk premium of the efficient portfolio

errors.label: Stopped at the risk premium
errors.explain: The CML gives the excess return; add R_F back to get E[R_A].

errors.label: Scaled the market return, not its premium
errors.explain: Scale the premium: (σ_A/σ_M)(E[R_M] − R_F), then add R_F.

questions.explanation: CML: E[R_A] = R_F + [(E[R_M] − R_F)/σ_M] σ_A. It applies to efficient portfolios only.

questions.stem: Wetaskiwin Pension Plan can mix T-bills (R_F = 3.0%) with the market portfolio (E[R_M] = 10.0%, σ_M = 16.0%). It wants an expected return of 8.5% per annum. Using the CML, what σ (% per annum) will the plan bear?

steps.label: Weight in M = target premium ÷ market premium

solution: CML: E[R] = R_F + [(E[R_M] − R_F)/σ_M] σ, so σ = σ_M × (E[R] − R_F)/(E[R_M] − R_F)

errors.label: Scaled the raw returns
errors.explain: Work with premiums: (8.5 − 3.0)/(10.0 − 3.0) of σ_M.

errors.label: Multiplied by the slope instead of dividing
errors.explain: σ = premium ÷ slope. Multiplying gives a number with the wrong units.

questions.explanation: On the CML the premium is the slope times σ, so σ = premium ÷ slope. The plan holds 78.6% M and 21.4% T-bills.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes the capital market line (CML) from the security market line (SML)?
options: The CML plots E[R] against β for all assets; the SML plots E[R] against σ for efficient portfolios only
The CML plots E[R] against σ for efficient portfolios only; the SML plots E[R] against β for every asset
Both plot E[R] against σ, but the SML starts at R_F while the CML starts at the origin
The CML has slope E[R_M] − R_F, while the SML has slope (E[R_M] − R_F)/σ_M
questions.explanation: CML: horizontal axis σ, slope = Sharpe ratio of M = (E[R_M] − R_F)/σ_M, efficient portfolios only. SML: horizontal axis β, slope = market risk premium E[R_M] − R_F, all assets. Giving the CML the slope E[R_M] − R_F and the SML the slope (E[R_M] − R_F)/σ_M swaps the two.

questions.stem: R_F = 3%. The market portfolio has E[R_M] = 10% and σ_M = 14%. A balanced fund has E[R] = 7% and σ = 12%. What follows?
options: It lies on the CML, because its 7% return exceeds R_F and its σ is below the market's σ
It beats the market portfolio, because its σ of 12% is lower than the market's 14%
Its Sharpe ratio is 0.33 against the market's 0.50, so it plots below the CML (M plus T-bills earns 9% at σ = 12%)
It is undervalued, because it plots below the CML and so offers a high return for its risk
questions.explanation: Sharpe_fund = (7 − 3)/12 = 0.33; Sharpe_M = (10 − 3)/14 = 0.50. At σ = 12% the CML gives 3 + 0.50 × 12 = 9%, so the fund is dominated. Below the CML means inefficient, not 'undervalued': that vocabulary belongs to the SML.

questions.stem: Which statement about the Sharpe ratio is NOT correct?
options: It equals the slope (tan φ) of the CAL through the portfolio
Its denominator is the portfolio's standard deviation
The portfolio with the highest Sharpe ratio has the best CAL
It measures the excess return earned per unit of beta
questions.explanation: Excess return per unit of β is the SML's reward-to-risk ratio. The Sharpe ratio divides the excess return by σ, equals tan φ, and ranks CALs: steeper is better.

questions.stem: Why is the best CAL the one tangent to the efficient frontier?
options: It touches the frontier at the lowest-σ portfolio, so it carries the least risk of any CAL
It has the steepest slope (highest Sharpe ratio) of any line from R_F that still touches an attainable portfolio
It is the only CAL that is a straight line, because it meets the frontier at just a single point
It has the highest intercept on the vertical axis, so it pays the most when σ = 0
questions.explanation: Every CAL starts at R_F, so the intercept is the same. A steeper line gives more return for each unit of σ; any line steeper than the tangent one misses all attainable portfolios. Tangency is about the highest slope, not the lowest σ.

questions.stem: R_F = 3%, E[R_M] = 9% and σ_M = 15%. Stock Q has σ_Q = 30% and β_Q = 0.8. An analyst plugs σ_Q into the CML and gets 15%. What is Stock Q's required (expected) return under the right model?
questions.explanation: A single stock carries diversifiable risk, so the CML (efficient portfolios only) does not apply; its reward depends on β through the CAPM: 3% + 0.8 × (9% − 3%) = 7.80%. The CML gives 15.00%; forgetting to add R_F gives 4.80%; using β × E[R_M] instead of β × MRP gives 10.20%.

questions.stem: The CML gives the expected return of an efficient portfolio A as E[R_A] = R_F + _____ × σ_A.
options: (E[R_M] − R_F)/σ_M
(E[R_M] − R_F)/σ_M²
E[R_M]/σ_M
(E[R_M] − R_F) × β_A
questions.explanation: The CML slope is the Sharpe ratio of the market portfolio, (E[R_M] − R_F)/σ_M. Dividing by σ_M² mixes units; omitting R_F uses the raw market return instead of its premium; multiplying by β_A turns it into the SML.

questions.stem: Banff Balanced Fund has E[R] = 8.6% and σ = 11.0%; its beta is 0.90. The market portfolio has σ_M = 14.0% and T-bills yield 2.0%. What is the fund's Sharpe ratio?
questions.explanation: Sharpe = (E[R_P] − R_F)/σ_P = (8.6 − 2.0)/11.0 = 0.60. Skipping R_F gives 0.78; dividing by β gives 7.33 (that is a reward-to-risk ratio, not a Sharpe ratio); dividing by the market's σ gives 0.47.

questions.stem: R_F = 3%. Portfolio P has E[R_P] = 11% and σ_P = 20%. An investor puts 60% in P and 40% in T-bills. What is the Sharpe ratio of her mixed position?
questions.explanation: The mix has E[R] = 0.6 × 11 + 0.4 × 3 = 7.8% and σ = 0.6 × 20 = 12%, so Sharpe = (7.8 − 3)/12 = 0.40, the same as P's own (11 − 3)/20 = 0.40: mixing with R_F slides you along the same CAL. Skipping R_F gives 0.65; using P's σ gives 0.24; mixing P's premium with the mix's σ gives 0.67.

questions.stem: R_F rises from 2% to 3% while E[R_P] and σ_P stay the same. What happens to the Sharpe ratio of P?
options: It rises, because R_F is part of the numerator
It is unchanged, because σ_P is unchanged
It falls only if β_P is greater than 1
It falls, because the numerator E[R_P] − R_F shrinks
questions.explanation: Sharpe = (E[R_P] − R_F)/σ_P. A higher R_F reduces the excess return while σ_P stays put, so the ratio falls (the CAL starts higher but is flatter). β plays no part in the Sharpe ratio.

questions.stem: The market portfolio has the highest Sharpe ratio of all risky portfolios on the efficient frontier.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. M is where the CAL from R_F is tangent to the frontier, which is the steepest attainable line, so its Sharpe ratio is the maximum.

questions.stem: The market portfolio M is best described as:
options: the portfolio at the far left of the frontier, with the lowest σ of all
the tangency portfolio, where the CAL from R_F touches the frontier (highest Sharpe ratio)
the single stock with the highest expected return, at the far right of the diagram
the risk-free asset combined 50/50 with the best-performing single stock
questions.explanation: M is the tangency portfolio: it has the steepest attainable CAL, i.e. the highest Sharpe ratio. The lowest-σ portfolio is the minimum-variance portfolio at the left end of the frontier, and the highest-return asset sits at the far right.

questions.stem: Starting at R_F on the vertical axis, an analyst rotates a straight line upward until it just touches the efficient frontier at a single point. The point of contact is the:
options: minimum-variance portfolio
risk-free asset
market portfolio M
portfolio with the highest expected return
questions.explanation: The first point the rotating line touches is the tangency point, and the line is the CML. The minimum-variance portfolio is the leftmost point of the frontier; the line from R_F does not touch it at its steepest.

questions.stem: Why do practitioners use a broad index such as the S&P 500 (SPDR trust) as a proxy for the market portfolio?
options: An index has σ = 0, so it works as a risk-free substitute for the true M
An index has been proven to lie exactly on the efficient frontier at the point of tangency
Investors are legally barred from holding M directly, so a proxy is required
M cannot be observed in advance, and the best past portfolio need not be the best future one
questions.explanation: It is hard enough to find the best portfolio from past data and even harder to predict where M will be, so we use a broad market index. An index is diversified but not risk-free, and nobody has proven it sits exactly at the tangency.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly separates the market portfolio from the minimum-variance portfolio?
options: M maximizes the Sharpe ratio; the minimum-variance portfolio minimizes σ
M minimizes σ; the minimum-variance portfolio maximizes the Sharpe ratio
Both describe the same point, the leftmost one on the efficient frontier
M is the highest-return frontier portfolio; the minimum-variance portfolio has the best Sharpe ratio
questions.explanation: Two different criteria pick two different points: tangency (best slope from R_F) picks M, lowest σ picks the minimum-variance portfolio. By construction no frontier portfolio has a higher Sharpe ratio than M.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT true of the market portfolio M?
options: It lies on the efficient frontier at the point where the CML touches it
Its beta is 1, so it carries the market's systematic risk
It has the lowest σ of any portfolio on the efficient frontier
It has the highest Sharpe ratio of any risky portfolio
questions.explanation: Lowest σ describes the minimum-variance portfolio. M is the tangency portfolio: on the frontier, β_M = 1, and the highest Sharpe ratio.

questions.stem: Two Calgary investors, one cautious and one bold, both accept the CML theory. How will their portfolios differ?
options: The cautious investor holds a lower-σ stock portfolio, while the bold one holds M
Both hold M; the cautious one holds more R_F (w_F > 0), the bold one less or borrows (w_F < 0)
The cautious investor holds only R_F and the bold investor holds only M itself
Each holds a different tangent portfolio, matched to the investor's own risk tolerance
questions.explanation: Every point on the CML is a mix of M and R_F, so risk tolerance only changes the weight w_F. There is one tangent portfolio, not one per investor.

questions.stem: Three portfolios on the efficient frontier have Sharpe ratios of 0.52, 0.61 and 0.58. M is the tangency portfolio. What can we conclude?
options: M's Sharpe ratio is 0.52, the lowest of the three, because M carries the least risk
M's Sharpe ratio is exactly 0.58, the middle of the three values, as the market is average
M's Sharpe ratio is at least 0.61, and the 0.61 portfolio offers the steepest CAL of the three
M's Sharpe ratio is below all three, because the index used to proxy M is imperfect
questions.explanation: M has the highest Sharpe ratio of all risky portfolios, so its ratio is at least as high as each of these three; of the three, the 0.61 portfolio gives the steepest CAL. M is not the minimum-risk portfolio, and an imperfect index proxy does not lower M's own ratio.

questions.stem: Which sequence describes how the market portfolio is found?
options: Plot the frontier → mark R_F → draw the steepest line from R_F that still touches the frontier → read off the tangency point as M
Mark R_F → pick the single stock with the highest expected return → draw a line from R_F to it → call that stock M
Plot the frontier → find its leftmost point (lowest σ) → draw a horizontal line across to R_F → call the point M
Mark R_F → draw the flattest line that touches the frontier → read off the contact point as M → plot the frontier afterwards
questions.explanation: M is found by tangency: first the frontier, then R_F, then the steepest CAL that still touches an attainable portfolio. The flattest line has the lowest Sharpe ratio and the leftmost point is the minimum-variance portfolio.

questions.stem: The market portfolio is the portfolio on the efficient frontier with the lowest σ.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. The lowest-σ portfolio on the frontier is the minimum-variance portfolio. The market portfolio is the tangency portfolio, with the highest Sharpe ratio.

questions.stem: In practice we proxy the market portfolio with a broad market _____, such as the S&P 500 (SPDR trust).
options: index portfolio
Treasury bill
dividend stock
bond ladder
questions.explanation: M cannot be observed in advance, so the course uses a broad market index portfolio (S&P 500, SPDR trust; in Canada the S&P/TSX Composite) as the stand-in.

questions.stem: Why does the market portfolio have a beta of exactly 1?
options: Because ρ = 1 and any perfectly correlated asset has β = 1
Because β is defined by setting the market's σ equal to 100%
Because β is measured relative to the risk-free asset, whose gross return is 1
β_M = cov(R_M, R_M)/σ_M² = σ_M²/σ_M² = 1: the market has the same risk as itself
questions.explanation: Beta is cov(R_i, R_M)/σ_M². Put i = M and the covariance of a variable with itself is its variance, so β_M = 1. A perfectly correlated asset has β = σ_i/σ_M, which equals 1 only if its σ matches the market's.

questions.stem: A Calgary advisor tells every client, cautious or bold: 'You will all hold the same low-cost broad index fund; we only change how much T-bill you hold alongside it.' Which idea underlies this advice?
options: Every investor holds the market portfolio plus the risk-free asset and differs only in w_F
Every investor should hold the minimum-variance portfolio, whatever their risk tolerance
Diversification eliminates systematic risk, so an index fund is risk-free
Each investor should pick a different single stock whose β matches their risk tolerance
questions.explanation: This is the CML idea: the best risky portfolio is the same for all (M, proxied by an index), and risk tolerance is expressed through the risk-free weight. An index fund still carries systematic risk.

questions.stem: A broad index fund such as the SPDR trust is only a proxy for the market portfolio, not M itself.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. The theoretical M uses expected returns and σ's we cannot observe in advance, so a broad index is used as a practical stand-in.

questions.stem: Systematic risk is risk that:
options: is unique to one company and disappears in a large portfolio
arises only from choosing poor weights for the stocks in a portfolio
affects almost all assets and cannot be removed by diversification
is borne only by investors who hold the risk-free asset
questions.explanation: Systematic (market, non-diversifiable) risk comes from surprises that hit nearly every asset, such as GDP, inflation and interest rates. Risk unique to a company is unsystematic.

questions.stem: The Bank of Canada unexpectedly raises its policy rate by 0.75 percentage points. For a stock portfolio this surprise is:
options: unsystematic risk, because only one institution made the decision
systematic risk, because it affects almost every firm
unsystematic risk, because only banks are affected
no risk at all, because the decision was announced publicly
questions.explanation: Interest rates are a classic market-wide factor, so a surprise change is systematic. Announcement does not remove risk; only the expected part of news is already priced.

questions.stem: A fire shuts down the only plant of Foothills Packaging Ltd. for six months. For an investor who also owns 40 other stocks, this event is mainly:
options: systematic risk, because the stock trades on the TSX
systematic risk, because every investor in the stock is affected
no risk at all, because the 40 other stocks are unaffected
unsystematic risk, because it is specific to one company
questions.explanation: A single-company event is company-specific (unsystematic, diversifiable) risk: with 40 other stocks it barely moves the portfolio. It is still a risk for that one stock, so 'no risk at all' overstates it.

questions.stem: A sudden pandemic lockdown cuts sales in nearly every Canadian industry at once. Which type of risk does this represent?
options: unsystematic risk, since it started with one virus
company-specific risk, since each firm is affected separately
systematic (market) risk, because it hits almost every firm at once
diversifiable risk, since it could be avoided by holding many stocks
questions.explanation: The shock hits almost all assets in the same direction, so holding many stocks does not cancel it: systematic, non-diversifiable risk.

questions.stem: Which of these events is mostly SYSTEMATIC risk?
options: The CEO of Sunrise Dairy resigns suddenly
A union strike halts one airline's flights
A data breach hits one retailer
Canadian inflation unexpectedly jumps to 8%
questions.explanation: An inflation surprise affects wages, costs and prices across the whole economy. The other three events are unique to one company, so they are unsystematic.

questions.stem: Which pair gives two names for the same type of risk?
options: Company-specific risk and diversifiable risk
Market risk and diversifiable risk
Systematic risk and company-specific risk
Unsystematic risk and non-diversifiable risk
questions.explanation: Company-specific = unsystematic = diversifiable = idiosyncratic. Market = systematic = non-diversifiable. The wrong pairs each mix one term from each family.

questions.stem: Which type of risk earns a risk premium in the CAPM framework?
options: Both types, with the premium proportional to the asset's total risk σ
Only unsystematic risk, because it is the risk investors choose to take
Only systematic risk, since unsystematic risk can be removed almost free
Neither type; the premium compensates investors only for expected inflation
questions.explanation: The systematic risk principle: the reward for bearing risk depends only on systematic risk. Unsystematic risk is avoidable by diversifying, so the market pays nothing for it.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT another name for unsystematic risk?
options: Idiosyncratic risk
Market risk
Diversifiable risk
Company-specific risk
questions.explanation: Market risk is a synonym for systematic risk. Company-specific, diversifiable and idiosyncratic risk all describe the unsystematic part.

questions.stem: Why does diversification fail to remove systematic risk?
options: Because investors cannot afford enough different stocks to cover the whole market
A systematic shock moves almost all assets the same way, so it does not cancel
Diversification only works when a portfolio holds fewer than ten stocks
Systematic risk is always smaller than unsystematic risk, so it never matters
questions.explanation: Unsystematic surprises are good for some stocks and bad for others, so they average out. A market-wide surprise moves everything together, so the portfolio σ bottoms out at about σ_M.

questions.stem: Why does the market pay no risk premium for unsystematic risk?
options: It is far too small to measure reliably, so the market simply ignores it
It is already built into the risk-free rate that every investor receives
Investors can remove it almost free by diversifying, so bearing it earns nothing
It is too uncertain to price, so the market leaves it out of expected returns
questions.explanation: Because unsystematic risk can be diversified away for free, the market does not reward risk borne unnecessarily. Only systematic risk, which cannot be removed without giving up expected return, earns a premium.

questions.stem: Moraine Holdings owns 8 Alberta energy stocks and adds 40 stocks spread across Canadian sectors. Which part of its risk falls the most?
options: Unsystematic risk; what remains is mostly systematic, close to σ_M
Systematic risk, because more stocks mean less market exposure
Both parts fall by the same proportion as stocks are added
Neither: adding stocks changes only expected return
questions.explanation: Spreading across sectors cancels company- and industry-specific surprises (unsystematic). The market-wide part stays, so σ_P falls toward the limit σ_M.

questions.stem: In the textbook's classic study of randomly chosen NYSE stocks (Table 13.7), equally weighted portfolios have an average σ of about 49% with 1 stock, 24% with 10, 20% with 100 and 19% with 1,000. What does the roughly 19% floor represent?
options: Unsystematic risk left over because 1,000 stocks is still too few
The risk-free rate, which is the return when all risk is removed
Systematic risk: about the market's own σ, which cannot be diversified away
Estimation error from using historical data to measure σ
questions.explanation: The drop from 49% to 19% is mostly unsystematic risk being diversified away; the benefit shrinks as stocks are added and flattens at the market's own volatility. A floor that does not fall further is systematic.

questions.stem: Total risk can be split into systematic risk plus unsystematic risk, and diversification removes only the unsystematic part.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Total risk = systematic + unsystematic. Diversifying cancels company-specific surprises, leaving the systematic part.

questions.stem: If a portfolio holds enough stocks, diversification eliminates both unsystematic and systematic risk.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Diversification eliminates only unsystematic risk. A very large portfolio still has σ close to σ_M because systematic risk affects all stocks.

questions.stem: As more stocks are added, the σ of a portfolio falls toward a limit of _____, the volatility of the market.
options: R_F
zero
σ_M
the σ of the lowest-σ stock in the portfolio
questions.explanation: The limit is σ_M, the systematic risk that cannot be diversified away. It does not reach zero, and it has nothing to do with R_F.

questions.stem: The textbook splits a stock's actual return into its expected return plus a systematic (market-wide) surprise and an unsystematic (company-specific) surprise. Fraser Foods is expected to return 7.0% this year. A market-wide surprise adds 2.0% and a company-specific surprise subtracts 3.5%. What is its actual return?
questions.explanation: R = E(R) + m + ε, where m is the systematic surprise and ε the unsystematic one: 7.0 + 2.0 − 3.5 = 5.50%. Ignoring the company-specific surprise gives 9.00%; adding the negative surprise as a positive gives 12.50%; ignoring the market-wide surprise gives 3.50%.

questions.stem: The Bank of Canada raised its policy rate by exactly the 0.25 percentage points that every analyst had expected, and Canadian stock prices barely moved. Why?
options: Interest rate changes are unsystematic, so they should not move market prices
Stock prices do not depend on interest rates, only on company earnings
Diversified portfolios are immune to systematic risk, so index prices cannot react
Only the surprise part of news moves prices; the expected part was already priced in
questions.explanation: Risk comes from surprises, the unanticipated part of the return. An expected change has already been discounted. Interest rates are systematic, and diversified portfolios still carry systematic risk.

questions.stem: Which statement about variance is correct?
options: Both a stock's and a diversified portfolio's variance measure only systematic risk
A single stock's variance measures total risk; a diversified portfolio's mostly systematic risk
Both a stock's and a diversified portfolio's variance measure only unsystematic risk
A diversified portfolio's variance reflects unsystematic risk; a stock's reflects systematic risk
questions.explanation: The variance of an individual asset includes both parts. In a well-diversified portfolio the unsystematic parts have washed out, so what is left is essentially the systematic risk.

questions.stem: The beta of stock i is defined as:
options: cov(R_i, R_M)/σ_M, the covariance per unit of market standard deviation
cov(R_i, R_M)/σ_M², the slope of the regression of stock returns on market returns
cov(R_i, R_M)/(σ_i σ_M), the correlation between stock and market
σ_i/σ_M, the ratio of the stock's volatility to the market's volatility
questions.explanation: β_i = cov(R_i, R_M)/σ_M² = ρ_iM σ_i/σ_M. Dividing by σ_M alone is the classic slip; dividing by σ_i σ_M gives the correlation ρ; σ_i/σ_M is only part of the ρ-version.

questions.stem: A regression of Cobalt Tech's monthly returns on the S&P/TSX Composite's monthly returns gives a slope of 1.6. How is the stock classified?
options: Aggressive: β > 1, more systematic risk than the market
Defensive: 0 < β < 1, less systematic risk than the market
Market-neutral: β = 0, no systematic risk at all
Opposite to the market: β < 0, moves against it
questions.explanation: The regression slope is β. A slope of 1.6 means the stock tends to move 1.6% for each 1% market move: more systematic risk than the market, so aggressive (typical of high tech).

questions.stem: Which asset would you expect to have a beta closest to zero?
options: A broad S&P/TSX Composite index fund
A high-growth software stock
A 91-day Government of Canada T-bill
A leveraged fund on the S&P 500
questions.explanation: The risk-free asset has no systematic risk, so β_F = 0. The broad index fund has β ≈ 1; growth and leveraged funds have β above 1.

questions.stem: Aurora Aerospace's return depends on the economy. Strong (probability 0.30): Aurora 30%, S&P/TSX Composite 22%. Moderate (0.50): Aurora 8%, market 9%. Weak (0.20): Aurora −16%, market −15%. Treating the index as the market, what is Aurora's beta?
keystrokes: Cov: sum of p × (deviation of stock) × (deviation of market) = 0.020262
Var: sum of p × (deviation of market)² = 0.016509; ÷ → 1.2273 → 1.23

errors.label: Divided the covariance by σ_M instead of σ_M²
errors.explain: The denominator is the market VARIANCE σ_M². Dividing by σ_M leaves a number that is not a beta.

errors.label: Computed the correlation instead of beta
errors.explain: Dividing the covariance by σ_i σ_M gives ρ, which cannot exceed 1. Beta divides by σ_M².

errors.label: Divided the covariance by the stock's variance
errors.explain: Beta measures sensitivity to the market, so the denominator is the market's variance, not the stock's.

questions.explanation: Beta is the covariance of the stock with the market divided by the market's variance; Aurora has 23% more systematic risk than the market.

questions.stem: Over five years, Muskoka Brewing's returns have a correlation of 0.72 with the S&P/TSX Composite. Muskoka's σ is 31% and the index's σ is 19%. What is Muskoka's beta?

errors.label: Reported the correlation as the beta
errors.explain: Correlation is bounded by ±1 and ignores relative size. Beta multiplies ρ by σ_i/σ_M.

errors.label: Inverted the volatility ratio
errors.explain: The stock's σ goes in the numerator and the market's in the denominator.

errors.label: Used σ_i/σ_M without ρ
errors.explain: Beta = ρ × σ_i/σ_M; the ratio alone ignores how tightly the stock follows the market.

questions.explanation: β = ρ σ_i/σ_M: Muskoka swings 1.63 times as much as the market but is only 72% correlated with it, giving β = 1.17.

questions.stem: Kootenay Foods' returns have a covariance of 0.0240 with the market's returns. The market's σ is 18%. What is Kootenay's beta?

errors.label: Divided by σ_M instead of σ_M²
errors.explain: Divide by the variance 0.0324, not the standard deviation 0.18.

errors.label: Inverted the ratio
errors.explain: The covariance goes on top: β = cov/σ_M².

questions.explanation: Beta is covariance over market variance; Kootenay is a defensive stock (β < 1).

questions.stem: Yukon Gold Corp. is a mining stock. In four equally likely states the market returns 20%, 8%, −4% and −16%, while Yukon Gold returns −6%, 0%, 6% and 18% respectively. What is Yukon Gold's beta?
solution: β = −0.0117/0.0180 = −0.65: the stock tends to move against the market
keystrokes: Cov: ¼ × Σ(dev stock × dev market) = −0.0117

errors.label: Divided the covariance by σ_M instead of σ_M²
errors.explain: The denominator is the variance 0.0180, not the standard deviation 0.1342.

errors.label: Computed the correlation instead of beta
errors.explain: Dividing by σ_i σ_M gives ρ (here −0.98). Beta divides by σ_M².

questions.explanation: A negative covariance with the market gives a negative beta: the stock does well when the market does badly (a rare, diversifying profile, like gold stocks in a scare).

questions.stem: A regression of 60 monthly returns gives Cobalt Tech: R_stock = 0.3% + 1.32 × R_market. If the market returns +4.0% next month, what return does the regression predict for Cobalt Tech (% per month)?
solution: The slope of the regression line is β = 1.32; the intercept is α = 0.3%

errors.label: Left out the intercept α
errors.explain: The regression line is α + β R_M; the stock's own average adds 0.3%.

errors.label: Divided by beta instead of multiplying
errors.explain: Beta is the slope: the stock moves β units per unit of market move, so multiply.

questions.explanation: Beta is the slope of the regression of stock returns on market returns: each 1% market move predicts a 1.32% move in the stock, plus the intercept.

questions.stem: Glacier Mining has σ = 36% and a correlation of 0.55 with the S&P/TSX Composite, whose σ is 22%. What is Glacier's beta?
questions.explanation: β = ρ σ_i/σ_M = 0.55 × 36/22 = 0.90. Reporting ρ as beta gives 0.55; inverting the σ ratio gives 0.34; dropping ρ gives 1.64.

questions.stem: Willow Utilities has a covariance of 0.0192 with the market. Willow's σ is 24% and the market's σ is 16%. What is Willow's beta?
questions.explanation: β = cov/σ_M² = 0.0192/0.0256 = 0.75. Dividing by σ_M gives 0.12; dividing by σ_i σ_M gives the correlation, 0.50; inverting the ratio gives 1.33.

questions.stem: Gold-Rush Royalty has σ = 45% and a correlation of −0.60 with the market, whose σ is 18%. What is its beta?
questions.explanation: β = ρ σ_i/σ_M = −0.60 × 45/18 = −1.50. Beta is not bounded by −1: it can be below −1 when the stock's σ exceeds the market's. Reporting ρ gives −0.60; inverting the σ ratio gives −0.24; dropping the sign gives 1.50.

questions.stem: Which statement about beta and the correlation coefficient ρ is correct?
options: ρ is bounded by −1 and +1, but β is not, since β also depends on σ_i/σ_M
Both are bounded by −1 and +1, since both measure co-movement with the market
β measures the strength of the linear association; ρ measures sensitivity to the market
They are always equal whenever the benchmark is the market portfolio itself
questions.explanation: Correlation only measures how tightly two return series move together. Beta rescales by σ_i/σ_M, so a stock twice as volatile as the market with ρ = 0.8 has β = 1.6.

questions.stem: Stock A has σ = 38% and β = 0.6. Stock B has σ = 21% and β = 1.4. Which statement is correct?
options: A has more systematic risk because its σ is higher
They have equal systematic risk because both trade on the same exchange
B has both more systematic risk and more total risk
B has more systematic risk; A has more total risk
questions.explanation: Beta measures systematic risk and σ measures total risk. A's extra volatility must be unsystematic, which a diversified investor can remove.

questions.stem: Which statement about beta is NOT correct?
options: The beta of any asset must lie between −1 and +1
The beta of the market portfolio is 1
The beta of a Treasury bill is 0
Beta is the slope of the regression of a stock's returns on the market's returns
questions.explanation: Only the correlation coefficient is bounded by ±1. Beta = ρ σ_i/σ_M can be 2.5 or −1.5 if the asset is much more volatile than the market.

questions.stem: Why can different information providers publish different betas for the same stock?
options: Beta reflects each investor's own risk aversion, which providers measure differently
Providers use different formulas, some dividing by σ_M and others by σ_M²
Beta is set by each company's management, not estimated from market returns
Each picks its own market index, estimation window, return frequency and adjustments
questions.explanation: Beta is estimated by regression from past returns, so every choice in the regression changes the answer. The formula cov/σ_M² is the same for all; beta is a property of the stock, not of the investor.

questions.stem: A fund has a beta of 1.4. If the market is expected to fall 10% in a sell-off, what does the beta imply (all else equal)?
options: A fall of about 7%
A fall of about 14% from the systematic component
A fall of 10%, since all diversified funds move with the market
A rise of 14%, since β > 1 means outperformance
questions.explanation: Beta is the sensitivity to the market: expected move ≈ β × market move = 1.4 × (−10%) = −14% (plus the fund's own α and noise).

questions.stem: Hollis Mining has a correlation of 0.95 with the market yet a beta of only 0.40. How is this possible?
options: It is impossible, because a stock with a correlation that high must have a beta close to 0.95
It has a very large unsystematic component that lowers its beta well below its correlation
Its σ is only about 0.42 times the market's, so it follows the market closely but swings far less
It has a large negative alpha, which pulls its beta below its correlation
questions.explanation: Solve 0.40 = 0.95 × σ_i/σ_M, so σ_i/σ_M = 0.42. High correlation says the stock follows the market; beta also scales for size. Alpha and unsystematic risk do not enter the formula.

questions.stem: Beta can be written β_i = ρ_iM × σ_i / _____.
options: σ_M²
σ_i
E[R_M] − R_F
σ_M
questions.explanation: β = cov/σ_M² and cov = ρ σ_i σ_M, so β = ρ σ_i σ_M/σ_M² = ρ σ_i/σ_M. The denominator is σ_M (not squared) in the ρ version.

questions.stem: The beta of a portfolio is:
options: the weighted average of the asset betas, with β = 0 for the risk-free asset
the square root of the weighted sum of the squared asset betas
the beta of the largest holding, since it dominates the portfolio
the simple, equal-weighted average of the risky assets' betas
questions.explanation: β_P = Σ w_i β_i with the same dollar weights used for the portfolio return, risk-free asset included at β_F = 0. An equal-weighted average ignores the actual weights.

questions.stem: What beta should a Government of Canada T-bill be given when you compute the beta of a portfolio that holds it?
options: 1, because it is part of the market
−1, because it offsets stocks
Its yield, expressed as a decimal
0, because it has no systematic risk
questions.explanation: The risk-free asset has β_F = 0, but its weight must still be included so that all weights sum to 1.

questions.stem: Lakeshore Family Office holds $12,000 in Nordic Utilities (β = 0.85), $20,000 in Harbour Bank (β = 1.15) and $8,000 in Aurora Aerospace (β = 1.55). What is the portfolio beta?
solution: Total = $40,000, so the weights are 0.30, 0.50 and 0.20

errors.label: Took the simple average of the betas
errors.explain: The portfolio is not equally weighted: the bank holds half the money.

errors.label: Paired the weights with the wrong stocks
errors.explain: Each beta must be multiplied by its own stock's weight.

questions.explanation: Portfolio beta is the dollar-weighted average of the stock betas: 1.14, more systematic risk than the market.

questions.stem: Parkland Wealth holds $22,000 in Stock A (β = 1.30), $18,000 in Stock B (β = 0.70) and $10,000 in T-bills. What is the portfolio beta?

errors.label: Dropped the T-bills and re-weighted the stocks over $40,000
errors.explain: T-bills have β = 0 but still take 20% of the weights; leaving them out overstates β_P.

errors.label: Gave the T-bills a beta of 1
errors.explain: The risk-free asset has no systematic risk: β_F = 0.

questions.explanation: The T-bills dilute the portfolio's beta: β_P = 0.82, a defensive portfolio.

questions.stem: Corvus Capital has $120,000 and wants a portfolio with a beta of 1.20. It already holds $30,000 in Stock X (β = 0.90) and $42,000 in Stock Y (β = 1.60). Stock Z has β = 1.25, and the rest of the money goes into a risk-free asset. How many dollars go into the risk-free asset?

errors.label: Set the risk-free weight to 1 − w_Z, ignoring X and Y
errors.explain: The risk-free weight is what remains after X, Y and Z: 1 − w_X − w_Y − w_Z.

errors.label: Solved for a beta of 1.00 instead of 1.20
errors.explain: The target is β_P = 1.20, not the market's 1.00.

questions.explanation: Set Σ w β equal to the target with β_F = 0, solve for the unknown weight, and let the risk-free asset take the rest: it absorbs $8,160.

questions.stem: A client of Ridgeline Advisors has $60,000 and wants a portfolio with a beta of 1.8. Ridgeline may use only one stock with β = 1.2 and a risk-free asset (equal lending and borrowing rates). What weight (%) goes into the risk-free asset? A negative answer means borrowing.
solution: She borrows 0.5 × $60,000 = $30,000 and invests $90,000 in the stock

errors.label: Entered the borrowing as a positive weight
errors.explain: A weight on the risk-free asset is negative when you borrow.

errors.label: Inverted the ratio: w_S = 1.2/1.8
errors.explain: A target beta above the stock's beta needs w_S > 1, so divide the target by the stock's beta.

errors.label: Subtracted the target beta from 1
errors.explain: The weights come from 1 − w_S, with w_S = target ÷ stock beta, not from the beta target itself.

questions.explanation: To reach a beta above any single stock's beta you must borrow at R_F: w_S = 1.5 and w_F = −0.5.

questions.stem: Delta Ridge Fund can mix Stock S (E[R] = 11.5%, β = 1.25) with T-bills yielding 3.5%. It wants the mix to have an expected return of 9.0%. What is the beta of the mix?

errors.label: Solved for the weight as 9.0/11.5
errors.explain: Work with premiums: w_S = (9.0 − 3.5)/(11.5 − 3.5).

errors.label: Used the T-bill weight as the weight on S
errors.explain: The weight on S is 0.6875; the T-bills get the remaining 0.3125.

questions.explanation: Return and beta are both linear in the weights, so the target return fixes w_S and then β_P = w_S β_S.

questions.stem: Yardley Fund holds four equal parts (25% each): T-bills, Stock Q (β = 1.10), Stock W (β = 0.70) and Stock X. The portfolio is exactly as risky as the market. What is Stock X's beta?

errors.label: Treated it as three equal parts, ignoring the T-bills' share
errors.explain: The T-bills occupy 25% of the weights with β = 0; it is a four-asset portfolio.

errors.label: Ignored the 25% weights altogether
errors.explain: Each beta is multiplied by its 0.25 weight before the sum equals 1.00.

questions.explanation: As risky as the market means β_P = 1. The T-bills contribute zero beta but take a quarter of the weights, so X needs a high beta.

questions.stem: Qualico Trust holds 40% in Stock A (β = 1.10), 35% in Stock B (β = 0.60) and 25% in T-bills. What is its portfolio beta?
questions.explanation: β_P = 0.40 × 1.10 + 0.35 × 0.60 + 0.25 × 0 = 0.44 + 0.21 = 0.65. Re-weighting over the stocks alone (forgetting the T-bill weight) gives 0.87; an equal-weight average gives 0.57; giving the T-bills a beta of 1 gives 0.90.

questions.stem: Orchard Capital has $75,000 of its own money, borrows $25,000 at the risk-free rate and invests the full $100,000 in stocks whose average beta is 1.20. What is the portfolio beta?
questions.explanation: Weights are measured on its own $75,000: w_stocks = 100/75 = 1.333 and w_F = −0.333, so β_P = 1.333 × 1.20 + (−0.333) × 0 = 1.60. Ignoring the leverage gives 1.20; using own money over total invested gives 0.90; adding the loan as 25% extra gives 1.50.

questions.stem: Brightwater Capital has a stock portfolio with β = 1.20. To cut its overall beta to 0.90 without changing the mix of its stocks, it moves part of the money into T-bills. What percentage of the portfolio goes into T-bills?
questions.explanation: β_P = w_S × 1.20 = 0.90, so w_S = 0.75 and the T-bills take 1 − 0.75 = 25.00%. Dividing the beta gap by the new beta gives 33.33%; using the raw beta gap gives 30.00%; reporting the stock weight kept gives 75.00%.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly contrasts portfolio beta with portfolio σ?
options: Both are simple weighted averages, so neither depends on correlations between assets
Portfolio beta is a weighted average of the betas; portfolio σ also depends on correlations
Portfolio σ is a simple weighted average, but portfolio beta needs correlations
Neither depends on the portfolio weights, only on the assets' own risks
questions.explanation: β_P = Σ w β is linear, like E[R_P]. σ_P is non-linear: the two-asset formula includes 2ρ w_A σ_A w_B σ_B, so diversification can push σ_P below the weighted average of the σ's.

questions.stem: To compute the beta of a portfolio of three stocks and a T-bill position, you do NOT need:
options: the correlations between the three stocks
each stock's beta
the portfolio weights, including the T-bill's
the fact that the T-bill has β = 0
questions.explanation: Beta is linear in the weights, so each asset's beta and weight is enough. Correlations among the holdings matter only for σ_P.

questions.stem: Why can a portfolio's beta be found as a weighted average of the betas, while its σ cannot?
options: Betas are always between 0 and 1, so they average neatly into a portfolio value
Beta ignores the risk-free asset, whereas σ_P includes it in the calculation
Beta is a covariance with the market and so linear in the weights; σ_P has cross terms
Beta is a pure number, while σ is measured in percent, so only beta can be averaged
questions.explanation: cov(R_P, R_M) = Σ w_i cov(R_i, R_M), so β_P = Σ w_i β_i. The portfolio variance has cross terms between every pair of assets, which is why σ_P is not a weighted average.

questions.stem: Orchard's stocks have an average beta of 1.00, but it holds 130% in stocks and −30% in the risk-free asset (borrowed). How should its portfolio beta be interpreted?
options: β_P = 1.00, because the borrowed money has β = 0 and changes nothing
β_P = 0.70, because borrowing 30% offsets 30% of the market risk
β_P cannot be computed because a negative weight has no beta
β_P = 1.30: borrowing makes the portfolio more aggressive than the market
questions.explanation: β_P = 1.30 × 1.00 + (−0.30) × 0 = 1.30. The loan itself has β = 0, but it allows 130% of own capital in stocks, which scales the systematic risk up.

questions.stem: A portfolio of risky stocks held with positive weights (no risk-free asset, no borrowing) can have a beta lower than the lowest beta among its stocks.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. The portfolio beta is a weighted average of the stock betas, so it lies between the smallest and largest. Only by adding the risk-free asset (β = 0) or short positions could it go below.

questions.stem: In β_P = Σ w_i β_i, the risk-free asset enters with a beta of _____.
options: its yield R_F
questions.explanation: The risk-free asset has no systematic risk, so β_F = 0. Its weight still counts in Σ w = 1.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly builds a portfolio with a target beta from some known holdings, one unknown stock and the risk-free asset?
options: Set w_F = 0 → solve for the unknown stock's weight → convert to dollars → check that Σ w β equals the target
Dollars to weights → Σ w β = target with β_F = 0 → solve for the unknown weight → w_F = 1 − the rest → back to dollars
Dollars to weights → set w_F = 1 − the unknown weight → solve for the unknown stock's beta → back to dollars
Solve for w_F first from E[R_P] → set β_F = 1 → average all the betas → convert weights to dollars
questions.explanation: The unknown stock's weight comes from the beta equation, and only then does the risk-free asset take the remainder (possibly negative). Fixing w_F first or giving it β = 1 breaks the logic.

questions.stem: If you invest in a stock which has a beta of 0.8, when the risk-free rate is 4.5% per annum and you expect the broad S&P 500 market index this year will return 10% per annum, what do you expect your stock return will be?

errors.label: Multiplied β by the whole 10% market return
errors.explain: 10% is the market's total return, not its premium. Subtract R_F first: the market risk premium is 10 − 4.5 = 5.5%.

errors.label: Left out the risk-free rate
errors.explain: 0.8 × 5.5 = 4.4% is only the reward for bearing risk. CAPM adds the time value of money R_F back.

errors.label: Applied β to the market return and dropped R_F
errors.explain: Two slips in one: the premium is E[R_M] − R_F, and R_F is then added to it.

questions.explanation: The market is expected to return 10% and T-bills pay 4.5%, so the market risk premium is 5.5%. With β = 0.8 the stock carries 80% of an average amount of systematic risk, so its premium is 4.4%. Add the risk-free rate: 8.9% per annum. The common trap is multiplying β by the 10% market return.

questions.stem: Government of Canada T-bills yield 3.4% per annum and the market risk premium is 6.2% per annum. Prairie Grid Utilities has a beta of 0.55. Using CAPM, what is its expected return? Answer in % per annum.

errors.label: Treated 6.2% as the market return and subtracted R_F again
errors.explain: The question gives the market risk premium, which already is E[R_M] − R_F. Subtracting R_F a second time understates the premium.

errors.label: Left out the risk-free rate
errors.explain: 3.41% is only the reward for risk. CAPM adds the time value of money R_F back.

errors.label: Added the full market risk premium without scaling by β
errors.explain: β = 0.55 means the stock carries only 55% of an average amount of systematic risk, so it earns only 55% of the premium.

questions.explanation: The market risk premium is given directly, so use it as is: E[R] = 3.4 + 0.55 × 6.2 = 6.81% per annum. A defensive utility (β < 1) earns less than the market.

questions.stem: Tundra Brewing is expected to return 9.1% per annum. T-bills yield 3.6% per annum and the market risk premium is 5.8% per annum. If CAPM holds, what is Tundra's beta? Give beta to 2 decimals.
solution: E[R] = R_F + β × MRP, so β = (E[R] − R_F)/MRP
